title: Retatrutide Benefits Beyond Weight Loss: What the 2026 Trial Data Actually Show
excerpt: Retatrutide's liver, knee, kidney, and lipid results, checked against the primary trial papers and sorted by how strong the evidence is.
seoTitle: Retatrutide Benefits Beyond Weight Loss: 2026 Trial Data
seoDescription: Retatrutide cleared liver fat in 93% of MASLD patients and cut knee pain by 75% in Phase 3 trials. We fact-check every claim against the primary sources.

children.text: Since 2023, retatrutide papers have reported effects on liver fat, knee pain, blood lipids, and kidney markers. Brain findings so far exist only in animals. Retatrutide is Eli Lilly's investigational GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist. No regulator has approved it. It is not a prescription drug. The only legal access is a registered clinical trial.
This article fact-checks the claims in Dr. Kevin Joseph's widely watched video,
"Retatrutide Isn't a Weight Loss Drug — Here's What It Really Does,"
against the primary trial sources under each claim, and grades each benefit by how strong the evidence is, from a published Nature Medicine substudy down to a single 2026 rodent study.
How this article grades the evidence
Not every claim about retatrutide sits on the same evidentiary footing. Before the data, here's how this article grades it:
Peer-reviewed, published data: the Phase 2 obesity trial (NEJM, 2023) and the Phase 2a MASLD liver-fat substudy (Nature Medicine, 2024).
Company-reported Phase 3 topline data: TRIUMPH-1 through TRIUMPH-4 press-release results, disclosed before full peer review.
Post-hoc surrogate-marker findings: kidney and lipid sub-analyses pulled from existing Phase 2 datasets after the fact.
Preclinical hypotheses: mechanism or animal-model findings not yet tested in a registered human trial.
Each section below names its evidence tier.
What retatrutide is

Retatrutide activates three hormone receptors from one weekly injection: GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon. Semaglutide (Wegovy/Ozempic) activates one of those; tirzepatide (Zepbound/Mounjaro) activates two. The third is the glucagon receptor, which researchers avoided for decades because glucagon's core job is to raise blood sugar. Phase 2 data suggest that, next to GLP-1 and GIP, it instead increases energy expenditure and pushes the liver to burn fat rather than store it. Trials tracked that with the ketone marker beta-hydroxybutyrate.

The three-receptor mechanism is real and published. Retatrutide itself is still investigational and available only inside Lilly's clinical trials. It is not for purchase or prescription under any name.
Retatrutide vs tirzepatide vs semaglutide

Cross-trial comparisons are not head-to-head data: each drug was tested in its own trial, in its own patient population, over a different follow-up length. With that caveat, the highest published weight-loss figures at each drug's top studied dose are:

Dr. Joseph's video correctly places retatrutide ahead of both comparators on published numbers, and correctly notes that Phase 2 weight loss had not plateaued by week 48. His TRIUMPH-4 figures (about 26% at 9 mg, 29% at 12 mg) round slightly higher than Lilly's reported 26.4% and 28.7%. Rounding, not a factual error.
Retatrutide's weight-loss magnitude leads its class on the numbers published so far, but no trial has tested all three drugs head-to-head in the same population.
Liver fat and MASLD

The Nature Medicine substudy (Sanyal et al., June 2024) is retatrutide's best-documented non-weight-loss result: in 98 participants with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), MRI-measured liver fat fell 82.4% at 24 weeks and 86.0% at 48 weeks on the 12 mg dose, versus a slight increase on placebo. By week 48, 93% of the 12 mg group reached normal liver fat (under 5%).

body.alt: Researchers reviewing a liver MRI related to retatrutide fatty liver findings in a diagnostic reading room
body.caption: MASLD evidence is MRI fat-fraction data, not a biopsy-proven fibrosis result. That gap still sits between this substudy and a liver-disease indication.

children.text: Dr. Joseph flags the limitation himself: the substudy did not take liver biopsies, so it cannot prove that fibrosis (scarring) reversed. It can show that fat content dropped and that fibrosis-related blood markers (ProC3, K18) moved favorably. One claim does need updating. The video describes MASLD/MASH as a disease "with no cure" in the US or Europe. That was true when the Phase 2a data were collected. The FDA granted accelerated approval to resmetirom (Rezdiffra) for MASH with fibrosis in March 2024, before this video was published. Patients with diagnosed MASH already have one FDA-approved option. Retatrutide's role in liver disease is still investigational and is being tested in SYNERGY-Outcomes (NCT07165028), a 4,500-person study comparing retatrutide and tirzepatide against placebo for major liver outcomes, with primary completion expected in 2030.

The liver-fat reduction is genuine, large, and published. It is a fat-content result. A dedicated fibrosis-outcome trial is still pending, and MASH already has one FDA-approved drug that retatrutide is not.
Knee osteoarthritis: TRIUMPH-4 pain results

TRIUMPH-4 (NCT05931367) enrolled 445 adults with obesity and knee osteoarthritis. At 68 weeks, the 12 mg dose cut WOMAC pain scores by about 4.4 points (roughly 75.8%) versus a 2.4-point drop on placebo, and roughly 1 in 8 retatrutide-treated participants reported being completely pain-free, versus about 1 in 24 on placebo.

body.alt: Physical therapist helping a patient climb stairs during a retatrutide knee arthritis mobility session
body.caption: TRIUMPH-4 measured walking and stair function as well as pain. The trial still cannot separate mechanical unloading from a direct joint effect.

children.text: These are topline, company-reported figures. Lilly has said detailed TRIUMPH-4 results are still pending conference presentation and peer-reviewed publication. Dr. Joseph flags this, noting the trial "can't fully separate" mechanical unloading of the joint from a possible direct anti-inflammatory effect. Until a weight-matched control arm or peer-reviewed subgroup analysis exists, read the knee-pain benefit as weight-loss-linked.

TRIUMPH-4's pain reduction is a real, prespecified trial result, but it is topline data, and it cannot yet be separated from the mechanical benefit of losing 25%+ body weight off a weight-bearing joint.
Lipids, blood pressure, and inflammation

Lilly's 2024 lipid substudy (338 participants, 48 weeks) reported reductions of up to 27% in non-HDL cholesterol, 24% in ApoB, 40.6% in triglycerides, and 36% in ApoC3 at the highest dose, alongside a shift toward larger, less-atherogenic LDL particles. TRIUMPH-4 separately reported a 14.0 mmHg drop in systolic blood pressure and reductions in high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) at the 12 mg dose.

These are legitimate, favorable surrogate-marker changes, but they remain surrogate markers. No completed retatrutide trial has yet reported a reduction in heart attacks, strokes, or cardiovascular death. That kind of hard-outcomes evidence is what a dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial is designed to produce; retatrutide's is the ongoing TRIUMPH-Outcomes trial (NCT06383390), tracking cardiovascular and kidney events through an estimated 2029 completion.
Favorable lipid, blood-pressure, and inflammation shifts are documented, but a cardiovascular protection claim remains a hypothesis awaiting TRIUMPH-Outcomes, not a proven benefit.
Kidney markers

A 2025 Kidney International Reports analysis (Heerspink et al.) pooled two completed Phase 2 trials (338 participants with overweight or obesity and 281 with type 2 diabetes) and re-examined kidney-related lab values collected for other purposes. In the obesity cohort, retatrutide 12 mg was linked to a 31.5% drop in urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) and an 8.5 mL/min/1.73m² rise in eGFR versus placebo at 48 weeks. In the diabetes cohort, UACR fell 37.0% but eGFR did not change.

This is a post-hoc analysis of existing markers, not a trial designed to test kidney outcomes, and the study authors said so directly, calling for dedicated follow-up. Lilly has since built that follow-up: TRANSCEND-CKD (NCT05936151), a completed Phase 2b mechanistic trial in adults with obesity and chronic kidney disease using gold-standard iohexol-clearance GFR measurement, and the ongoing TRIUMPH-Outcomes trial, which is tracking major kidney events directly.

The kidney-marker signal is real and dose-dependent. A post-hoc lab-value analysis does not establish that retatrutide prevents kidney failure. That is what TRIUMPH-Outcomes and TRANSCEND-CKD exist to test.
Brain and cognition

GIP and GLP-1 receptors are expressed in brain regions involved in memory and appetite, and a January 2026 rodent study reported that retatrutide protected learning and memory in diabetic rats while lowering brain inflammation. Dr. Joseph labels this correctly in his video, calling it "the least proven part of everything" he covers and noting that no human brain studies exist yet.

A rat study and an advocacy-foundation review are not evidence of a cognitive benefit in people. Any claim that retatrutide improves memory or brain health in humans is extrapolating from animal receptor biology, not citing a completed human trial.
The brain-signaling mechanism is a legitimate, active research question, but it remains a preclinical hypothesis, not a demonstrated human cognitive benefit.
What TRIUMPH-4 reported on safety

TRIUMPH-4's most common adverse events were gastrointestinal: nausea (up to 43.2%), diarrhea, constipation, and vomiting, generally dose-related and consistent with other incretin-class drugs. The trial also identified a signal largely absent from Phase 2: dysesthesia (tingling, burning, or abnormal skin sensation), reported in 20.9% of participants on 12 mg and 8.8% on 9 mg, versus 0.7% on placebo. Most cases were mild, peaked during dose escalation, and rarely caused discontinuation, but the pattern is steeply dose-dependent.
Discontinuation for any reason was similar between retatrutide and placebo. Discontinuation due to adverse events was higher on retatrutide (12.2%–18.2% vs. 4.0% on placebo).

The GI side-effect pattern mirrors other GLP-1/GIP drugs. The dysesthesia signal is a new Phase 3 finding, and it is one Dr. Joseph's video does not mention. FDA would scrutinize it in any future review.
Is retatrutide approved?

No. As of mid-2026, retatrutide has no FDA, EMA, or other regulatory approval for any indication. Lilly has reported five positive Phase 3 topline readouts (TRIUMPH-1 through TRIUMPH-4) and stated on July 23, 2026 that it plans to submit a Biologics License Application to the FDA in Q1 2027. That is a filing date, not an approval date. A standard FDA review adds roughly 10–12 months after filing, putting a realistic decision in late 2027 or 2028.

Topline press-release numbers are not peer-reviewed evidence. Every TRIUMPH-1 through TRIUMPH-4 figure in this article, in Dr. Joseph's video, and elsewhere online right now is a company-reported result awaiting full publication and independent statistical review.

Retatrutide remains investigational with a realistic approval window of 2027 or later. It is not available by prescription anywhere, and no product sold under that name outside a registered clinical trial is the studied compound.
What the video got right

Dr. Joseph's video is one of the more careful physician overviews of retatrutide's non-weight-loss data. He flags the liver-biopsy limitation, the knee-pain confound, and the preclinical status of the brain data. Two updates: the "no approved cure" MASH claim, superseded by resmetirom's 2024 approval, and the missing TRIUMPH-4 dysesthesia signal.

title: BPC-157 vs TB-500
excerpt: BPC-157 vs TB-500 is not two equivalent healing peptides. Most TB-500 human data belongs to full-length thymosin beta-4, a different molecule.
body:
Most BPC-157 vs TB-500 writeups treat them as two "healing peptides" in the same class. Ask a narrower question first: how much of what you have read comes from a study you could hand to a clinician? Not much. Neither peptide is FDA-approved. Both sit on the 2026 World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) Prohibited List at all times.

They are also not the same kind of object. BPC-157 is a defined 15-residue sequence. TB-500, on the research-chemical market, has been identified as a short fragment of a different protein. That changes which papers you can cite.

## Quick comparison

Origin: BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid pentadecapeptide modeled on a gastric protein fragment. TB-500 is marketed as thymosin beta-4 derived but was analytically identified as the acetylated 17-23 fragment (Ac-LKKTETQ). Molecular weight: BPC-157 is roughly 1,419 Da; the TB-500 fragment is roughly 888 Da versus roughly 4,963 Da for full-length thymosin beta-4. Best-supported evidence: BPC-157 has extensive animal and cell data on tendon and muscle angiogenesis; TB-500 human trials exist almost entirely for full-length recombinant thymosin beta-4, not the fragment sold under that name. Human data volume: fewer than 30 subjects across uncontrolled BPC-157 pilot work, per a 2026 pharmaceutical development review, versus Phase I safety data in 54 healthy volunteers for full-length thymosin beta-4. FDA compounding: both BPC-157 and the thymosin beta-4 fragment (LKKTETQ) were added to Category 2 significant safety risk lists in September 2023. WADA 2026: both are prohibited at all times (BPC-157 under S0 Non-Approved Substances; TB-500 under S2 Growth Factors as a thymosin beta-4 derivative).

## What you are actually comparing

BPC-157 is one sequence. TB-500 is a product name. Mass spectrometry in Drug Testing and Analysis looked at vials sold as TB-500 and found a molecule of 888.49 Da: the N-terminal acetylated 17-23 fragment of thymosin beta-4 (Ac-LKKTETQ). Full-length thymosin beta-4 is 43 amino acids, about 4,963 Da.

Most of the credible human work on thymosin beta-4 used the full-length recombinant protein: a Phase I dose-escalation trial in 54 healthy volunteers, a European randomized trial in venous leg ulcers, and cardiac trials after heart attack. Those papers do not test the seven-residue fragment. If a vendor cites a thymosin beta-4 heart or wound study to sell TB-500, they are moving evidence from one molecule onto a smaller one that was not in those trials.

Independent checks of research-market vials are still scarce. You cannot assume every bottle labeled TB-500 contains the same fragment at the same purity. That mix-up is how marketers borrow decades of a different molecule's clinical history.

## What the BPC-157 evidence shows

BPC-157's animal and cell-culture data are large. Studies have linked it to upregulated VEGF-driven angiogenesis in healing tendon and muscle, and to increased growth hormone receptor expression in Achilles tendon fibroblasts, which the authors proposed as one driver of the tendon-repair effects seen in rodents. A 2026 orthopaedic sports medicine systematic review found 36 studies through mid-2024: 35 preclinical, one clinical. That clinical paper was a retrospective case series. Seven of 12 patients with chronic knee pain reported symptom relief lasting more than six months after an intra-articular injection. No control group. No standardized product.

A separately registered human safety trial (NCT02637284) was never published. Reporting cited in an independent evidence review said its data were withdrawn before outside review. As of 2026, one placebo-controlled Phase 2 trial (BPC-HAMSTR, NCT07437547) is recruiting to test BPC-157 for acute hamstring strains. If it completes, it would be the first controlled human efficacy data for a musculoskeletal indication. Until then, claims that BPC-157 speeds tendon or ligament recovery in people rest on rodent models, not confirmed human outcomes.

## What the TB-500 / thymosin beta-4 evidence shows

Set the fragment-versus-protein issue aside and look at what has been tested. Full-length recombinant thymosin beta-4 has a real, if narrow, human safety record. A randomized Phase I study gave single and multiple intravenous doses to 54 healthy volunteers and reported only mild-to-moderate adverse events, with no dose-limiting toxicities. Topical thymosin beta-4 has been studied in a compassionate-use case series for chronic corneal defects (nine patients) and in a randomized European trial for venous leg ulcers. On the cardiac side, a completed Phase IIa trial (NCT05485818) and an upcoming Phase IIc trial (NCT07586865) are evaluating intravenous recombinant thymosin beta-4 after heart attacks, using cardiac MRI to measure infarct size.

None of those trials used the LKKTETQ fragment identified in TB-500 vials. None targeted the tendon, ligament, or soft-tissue injuries TB-500 is usually sold for in fitness and recovery communities. The mechanistic argument for the fragment rests on in-vitro cell-migration assays showing LKKTETQ can replicate some of the parent protein's actin-regulating activity. That finding is real. It is also one step removed from a clinical outcome in humans.

## Four questions before you trust a claim

Was this shown in a dish, an animal, or a person? If an animal, has anyone confirmed it in humans? If the human study used a different formulation (full protein vs fragment, or a pharmaceutical-grade compound vs an online vial), does the finding transfer? Has this specific product been independently verified to contain what the label claims?

Most loud claims fail at least one of those. For BPC-157 it is usually animal-to-human. For TB-500 it is usually full-protein-to-fragment.

## Safety and regulation

The FDA placed both BPC-157 and the thymosin beta-4 fragment (LKKTETQ) into Category 2 of its 503A bulk drug substance list in September 2023. Compounding pharmacies are not permitted to use either as an active ingredient. The agency cited immunogenicity risk for certain routes, unresolved peptide-impurity characterization, and insufficient safety data to determine whether the substances would harm humans. That is an absence of the data needed to rule harm out, not a finding that they are dangerous. Both substances are also prohibited at all times under WADA's 2026 Prohibited List. Any athlete subject to testing risks a sanction, including for cosmetic or off-label recovery use.

## If you are choosing based on evidence

BPC-157 has a large animal literature and almost no controlled human data. TB-500 looks safer in humans only if you treat it as full-length thymosin beta-4, which most vials may not be. Neither has been shown, in a controlled human trial, to do what it is commonly sold for.

For a soft-tissue injury, the option with actual evidence is still monitored rehabilitation: physical therapy, graded loading, and, where it fits, one of the registered trials. Not an unregulated research-chemical vial.

## FAQ

Is TB-500 the same as thymosin beta-4? No. Analytical testing identified TB-500 as a seven-amino-acid acetylated fragment of the 43-amino-acid thymosin beta-4 protein. Product labeling in the research-chemical market is inconsistent, so purity and identity are not independently guaranteed.

Are BPC-157 and TB-500 legal to buy? They are sold as research chemicals. The FDA has stated there is no legal basis for compounding pharmacies to use either in a prescription product, and both are banned in tested sports.

Is there any ongoing human research? Yes. A Phase 2 trial of BPC-157 for hamstring strains and Phase II trials of full-length recombinant thymosin beta-4 for heart attack recovery are both active.
